opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it really started with games. When I was a kid, like a lot of kids, I was fascinated by video games, but I wasn't satisfied just playing them. I kept wondering how they actually worked, how someone could make a character move on the screen or design the rules of a world. At some point the thought became, "What if I could make my own?"

That curiosity is what pushed me to start learning programming. In the beginning it was very basic: writing small programs, trying to draw things on the screen, making simple interactive stuff. Most of what I made was pretty crude, honestly, nothing like the games I admired. But the feeling of typing something and watching the computer respond, seeing an idea in your head come alive, was incredibly addictive.

Looking back, games were just the entry point. What really hooked me was the act of building things. Once I learned to program, I realized you can create almost anything with it. That sense of creation stayed with me, and later it carried into algorithms, machine learning, and building systems. Even now, building a framework or a system feels a lot like building a game: you design the rules, you put the pieces together, and then you see whether the whole thing actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says video games first sparked his interest in programming, then explains that building things with code became the lasting motivation and expanded into computing areas such as algorithms and machine learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started the way it does for a lot of kids. I was in school in Shanghai, I loved playing games, and at some point I stopped being satisfied with just playing them. I wanted to know how they worked, and more than that, I wanted to make my own.

So I picked up a book on programming, I think it was Pascal at first, and then C, and I just started trying to build little things. Text-based games, simple graphics, that kind of stuff. Most of it was terrible, of course. But what hooked me wasn't really the game itself. It was that moment where you type something, run it, and the computer actually does what you imagined. That feedback loop was addictive.

And I think that's really where my taste for systems came from. Making a game run smoothly forces you to care about performance, about memory, about how things fit together underneath. You can't just write the logic and hope. So without realizing it, I was learning the things that later mattered a lot for machine learning systems, where you're constantly asking how to make something run faster on the hardware you actually have.

The games never turned into anything, to be clear. But the habit of building things to understand them, and the joy of seeing something you wrote come alive on the screen, that stuck with me all the way through XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, and everything since.

r001.rationale: He says he first wanted to make games, then became hooked by making the computer do what he imagined and by learning how systems work, showing a shift toward computing itself.

astra-6.text: When I was younger, I really enjoyed playing video games, and I started wondering whether I could make one myself. But to do that, I needed to learn how to program. So programming was initially a means to an end: I wanted to create something I could play. What made it exciting was that I could write some code and see something happen. That process of building something, trying it out, and figuring out why it didn’t work drew me in, and gradually I became interested in programming itself.

r001.rationale: The response says he first learned programming to make a video game, then gradually became interested in programming itself.

sol-6.1.text: I got interested in programming because I wanted to make video games.
